lessons.title: એક, બે, ત્રણ, ચાર, પાંચ — one to five
lessons.gloss: one to five — the two numbers that don't look like their neighbours'

segments.text: Three of these will look familiar from any other Indian language. Two won't — and both have a reason.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the five

segments.text: Notice the script: Gujarati is Devanagari without the top line. Same letters, same system — the shirorekhā simply isn't drawn. If you've done the Hindi writing track you can feel the relationship immediately.

blocks.title: What you've built: two surprises and a headless script

segments.text: Most neighbouring languages have a d in “two,” but Gujarati says બે be. Hindi says tīn for “three,” but Gujarati says ત્રણ traṇ, with an r.
Do not carry both histories while the count is still new. Make the five forms automatic first; the next prerequisite-ordered lesson explains why be and traṇ took those shapes.

segments.text: Count to five in Gujarati. (Ek, be, traṇ, chār, pā̃ch.) Why does બે look unlike its neighbours? (It begins with b, not d.) What does ત્રણ contain that Hindi tīn does not? (r.) What is visibly missing from the Gujarati script? (The top line: the shirorekhā is not drawn.) Next: trace the two surprising number histories.

lessons.title: Two number histories: be and traṇ
lessons.gloss: why Gujarati two begins with b and why three regained an r

segments.text: Count once: ek, be, traṇ, chār, pā̃ch. Which two forms look least like Hindi or Marathi? (Be and traṇ.)

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — બે from a different ancestor

segments.text: Sanskrit had gendered forms of “two,” and its daughters selected different parts of that paradigm:

utterances: language: Sanskrit. “two”: dváu (masc.), dvé (fem. and neut.) route: —.
language: Hindi. “two”: do. route: masculine side.
language: Marathi. “two”: don. route: masculine side, plus an analogical -n.
language: Bengali. “two”: dui. route: disyllabic Prakrit duve.
language: Gujarati. “two”: be. route: feminine/neuter dvé side.

segments.text: Gujarati બે is not a corruption of do. It is a different inheritance from the same Sanskrit paradigm.

The initial cluster changed too. In dv-, the dental d adopted the labial place of the following v: dv becomes bb becomes b. The first consonant was remade in the shape of its neighbour, then the double simplified.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — ત્રણ and the r that came back

utterances: stage: Prakrit. “three”: tiṇṇi: r already gone.
stage: Gujarati. “three”: traṇ: r present again.

segments.text: The shared ṇ shows that Hindi and Gujarati both descend from neuter trī́ṇi through Prakrit tiṇṇi. By that stage, the r was gone and its weight had moved into doubled ṇṇ. Hindi later simplified the double and lengthened the vowel.

Gujarati's tr- is generally treated as restored from Sanskrit, not carried through unbroken. Sanskrit remained a literary language and continued to reshape its descendants. Traṇ looks older than tīn, but it is closer because speakers put the r back.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: inherited continuously or restored — restored]

segments.text: Why be, not Hindi do? (Different Sanskrit forms.) What changed in dv becomes b? (D became labial beside v; the double simplified.) Did traṇ keep r? (No: Sanskrit restored Prakrit's lost r.) How can a newer form look older? (Learned restoration.)

segments.prompt: Does Gujarati be descend from the same Sanskrit form as Hindi do?

feedback.correct: Right: Gujarati and Hindi selected different Sanskrit forms for two.
feedback.incorrect: No. Gujarati be and Hindi do descend from different Sanskrit forms.
